title: Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC)
subject: haematology-oncology
setting: Emergency department, oncology ward, primary care referral
summary: In a person with cancer, back pain with neurological symptoms is an emergency: give dexamethasone 16 mg at once, immobilise if instability is suspected, get whole-spine MRI within 24 hours, and arrange surgery or radiotherapy (within 24 hours) through the oncology or MSCC team.

sections.title: Recognise (NICE NG234)
items: Think of spinal metastases in anyone with past, current or suspected cancer who has severe unremitting or progressive back pain, mechanical pain, pain worse on coughing, sneezing or straining, night pain disturbing sleep, localised spinal tenderness, or leg claudication.

Features of cord compression: limb weakness, gait disturbance or difficulty walking, numbness, paraesthesia or sensory loss, radicular pain, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or other signs of cord or cauda equina compression.
Common primaries: breast, prostate, lung, kidney, myeloma and lymphoma. MSCC can be the first presentation of cancer.
Neurological outcome depends on function at the time of treatment: act before the patient stops walking.

sections.title: Immediate actions
items: Cancer plus symptoms or signs of cord compression: treat as an oncological emergency and contact the MSCC coordinator or oncology on-call immediately.
Cancer plus pain suggesting spinal metastases but no neurological features: seek advice within 24 hours; MRI within 1 week.
Neurological symptoms or signs: dexamethasone 16 mg orally (or equivalent IV) as soon as possible; do not wait for MRI.

Immobilise without delay (including for transfer) if neurological features suggest spinal instability; consider it for moderate to severe movement-related pain. Nurse supine, flat or with partial elevation, and log-roll.
Prompt analgesia (opioid and non-opioid, plus neuropathic agents if needed). Check for urinary retention and catheterise if present.
Suspected lymphoma or myeloma without neurological signs: get haematology advice before steroids, which can compromise the diagnosis.

sections.title: Investigations
items: MRI of the whole spine as soon as possible and always within 24 hours for suspected MSCC: sagittal T1 and/or STIR of the whole spine, sagittal T2, and axial images through any abnormality. Overnight MRI only if it would allow treatment to start immediately.
If MRI is contraindicated, CT of the spine. Do not use plain X-rays to diagnose or exclude spinal metastases or MSCC.
Baseline FBC, renal function, calcium (hypercalcaemia), liver function and glucose before steroids.
No known primary: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, PSA, serum protein electrophoresis with free light chains, and image-guided biopsy if it will change treatment and immediate treatment is not needed.
Use the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) for stability and a validated prognostic score (revised Tokuhashi) as part of a full clinical assessment.

sections.title: Definitive treatment
items: Plan urgently with the MSCC multidisciplinary team (oncologist and spinal surgeon).

Suitable patients: surgical decompression with or without stabilisation as soon as possible after neurological symptoms begin, guided by the speed of progression. Do not use time since paralysis alone to refuse surgery.
Offer stabilisation surgery (or an external orthosis if surgery is unsuitable) for spinal instability with mechanical pain not controlled by analgesia, even with severe neurological deficit.

MSCC not suitable for surgery: radiotherapy as soon as possible and within 24 hours, usually 8 Gy single fraction; multiple fractions if at high risk of side effects. Omit if complete paraplegia for 2 weeks or more with controlled pain, or poor overall prognosis.
Postoperative radiotherapy once recovered from surgery.
Haematological malignancy: dexamethasone 16 mg then further treatment agreed with the haematology team; radiotherapy may affect later stem cell harvest.

sections.title: Steroids and supportive care
items: Continue dexamethasone 16 mg daily while awaiting surgery or radiotherapy, then reduce gradually until stopped after surgery or from the start of radiotherapy. Stop it if MSCC is excluded.
While on dexamethasone: give a proton pump inhibitor and monitor capillary glucose, aiming for 108 to 180 mg/dL (6 to 10 mmol/L).
VTE prophylaxis (mechanical and, when safe, pharmacological), pressure area care, bladder and bowel care.
Myeloma or breast cancer with spinal involvement: bisphosphonates to reduce pain and vertebral collapse.
When imaging suggests the spine is stable: graded sitting then weight bearing, monitoring pain and neurology; return to the previous position and reassess if symptoms worsen.

sections.title: Rehabilitation and follow-up
items: Start rehabilitation and discharge planning on admission; offer specialist rehabilitation if likely to benefit.
Offer holistic needs assessment, advance care planning and end-of-life care when appropriate.
Teach patients with known spinal metastases the warning symptoms and how to seek urgent help.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Waiting for weakness or sphincter loss before imaging.
Imaging only the symptomatic level: multilevel disease is common, so scan the whole spine.
Plain X-rays used to rule out metastases.
Starting steroids before biopsy in suspected lymphoma without neurological deficit, or forgetting to taper steroids, give a PPI and monitor glucose.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.dose: 16 mg orally (or equivalent IV) immediately, then 16 mg daily until surgery or radiotherapy, then taper to stop
drugs.notes: Stop if MSCC excluded. Monitor glucose; give PPI.

drugs.name: Pantoprazole
drugs.dose: 40 mg orally once daily while on dexamethasone
drugs.notes: Any proton pump inhibitor is acceptable.

drugs.name: Zoledronic acid
drugs.dose: 4 mg IV over at least 15 minutes every 3 to 4 weeks
drugs.notes: Myeloma or breast cancer with spinal involvement. Reduce dose if CrCl 30 to 60 mL/min; avoid below 30. Check calcium and dental health.
